Think of "arrive at" as meaning to reach something — either a place or an answer. That's the heart of it. The phrase works in two big ways: in the real, physical world and in the world of thinking.
Meaning 1: To Reach a Physical Place

When you travel somewhere and you get there, you arrive at that place.

Examples:

  • We arrived at the hotel just before midnight.
  • She arrived at the bus stop too late and missed it.
  • The guests arrived at the wedding hall by 5 PM.

This is straightforward. You were somewhere else. You traveled. You got there. You arrived at it.
Meaning 2: To Reach a Conclusion, Decision, or Answer (Through Thinking)

This is the more important and widely used meaning. When you think deeply about a problem, discuss something with others, or study a situation carefully — and then finally reach an answer or a decision — you arrive at that conclusion or decision.

The idea is that your mind goes on a journey, just like your body does when you travel. Thinking is the road. The conclusion is the destination. When you finally get there, you have arrived at it.

Examples:

  • After hours of discussion, the committee arrived at a decision.
  • How did you arrive at that conclusion?
  • Scientists arrived at this result after years of research.
  • The two countries finally arrived at an agreement.
  • I sat with the problem for weeks before I arrived at a solution.

Notice that in every case, there is a process happening before the arrival. You don't just suddenly have an answer — you work toward it, think through it, or discuss it, and then you arrive at it. This sense of effort and journey is baked into the phrase.
"Arrive At" vs. "Arrive In" — A Key Distinction

This is one of the most important things to know, and many learners get confused here.

Use "arrive at" for specific, smaller locations — a building, a venue, an event, a place with a clear boundary.

  • arrive at the airport
  • arrive at school
  • arrive at the station
  • arrive at the conference
  • arrive at someone's house

Use "arrive in" for large areas — cities, countries, regions, or continents.

  • arrive in London
  • arrive in Japan
  • arrive in Europe
  • arrive in the north

Special case — "arrive home": When you arrive home, you use no preposition at all. You don't say "arrive at home." You simply say "I arrived home."

A simple way to remember this:

Small and specific = "at." Large and broad = "in." Home = nothing.
The Words That Most Commonly Go With "Arrive At" (Collocations)

In the figurative sense, "arrive at" is almost always followed by one of these words. Learning these combinations will make you sound natural:

  • Arrive at a conclusion — after thinking something through
  • Arrive at a decision — after weighing options
  • Arrive at an agreement — after negotiating
  • Arrive at a solution — after working on a problem
  • Arrive at an answer — after figuring something out
  • Arrive at a consensus — after a group discusses and agrees
  • Arrive at an understanding — after clearing up confusion between people
  • Arrive at a verdict — what a jury does at the end of a trial

These are the natural partners of "arrive at." When you see or hear this phrase, it will almost certainly be followed by one of these words.

You might wonder: can't you just say "reach a conclusion" instead of "arrive at a conclusion"? Yes, you can — they mean the same thing. But "arrive at" carries a slightly stronger sense of process and effort. It emphasizes that you traveled mentally or physically to get there. "Reach" is more neutral. In formal writing and speech, "arrive at" is very commonly preferred.
Register: When and Where Is This Phrase Used?

• In everyday speech, the literal meaning (arriving at places) is completely normal and casual.
  • The figurative meaning tends to be slightly more formal. You'll see it often in academic writing, news articles, business discussions, legal settings, and scientific papers. However, it also appears in everyday conversation without sounding stiff.

Mistake 1: Saying "arrive at" when you should say "arrive in."

❌ We arrived at France.
✅ We arrived in France.

Mistake 2: Saying "arrive to."

❌ She arrived to the station.
✅ She arrived at the station.

"Arrive to" is a very common error among learners. English does not use "to" after "arrive." Always use "at" or "in" depending on the size of the place.

Mistake 3: Saying "arrive at home."

❌ I arrived at home.
✅ I arrived home.

"Arrive at" is a phrase built on one powerful image: reaching a destination. Whether that destination is a building you walked into or a conclusion you thought your way into, the phrase captures the same thing — the end of a journey. In the physical world, you arrive at places. In the world of the mind, you arrive at answers, decisions, and agreements — but only after a real process of working through things.

Master this phrase and you will handle it correctly in both casual conversation and formal writing.
